steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our PreciseBugCollector paper, a tool for collecting a precise, executable bug-fix dataset. Cover why precise bug datasets matter, what's wrong with current ones, how our bug tracker and bug injection components work, and the resulting dataset and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Importance of precise bug datasets; two kinds of existing datasets
- Key challenges in collecting a useful bug dataset
- PreciseBugCollector and the bug information it provides
- Component 1: bug tracker
- Component 2: bug injection
- Data sources, resulting dataset and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Importance and current datasets
  - tasks: bug detection, fault localization, pattern mining, APR patch generation, patch assessment (cite each)
  - type 1: human curation, careful but small: ManyBugs and IntroClass, Defects4J, QuixBugs (cite); each fewer than 1 000 bugs
  - type 2: large-scale mined from repos, e.g. ManySStubBs4J (cite), text processing of commit messages/issues; imprecise, simple keyword comparison
  - still widely used for training data in academia (cite) and industry (cite): easy to build large datasets
- Challenges
  - P1 data quality vs scalability: manual = quality, no scale; keyword matching = scalable, imprecise (cite)
  - P2 language diversity: mostly single language; usability, external validity
  - P3 lack of metadata: usually commit ID/message; missing bug type, severity, date of discovery
  - P4 lack of tests: few datasets have tests exposing bug; reproduction and validating fixes beyond developer's
- PreciseBugCollector
  - tackles imprecision in bug dataset creation
  - accurate bug type + meta info: buggy code, fix code, precise location, error type, executable/reproducible tests
  - <bug,fix,loc,type,(test)>
- Bug tracker
  - extracts bug-fix commits; code repos (GitHub, Bitbucket, Gitlab, SVN) + bug repos (OSS-Fuzz, Jira, Apache Bug Report)
  - code repos: exact changes, no clear metadata; bug repos: metadata, not always exact changes
  - merge the two sources
- Bug injection
  - generates artificial unseen bugs, each exposed by existing test suite with at least one failing test
  - start from code with all tests passing; code noising tool introduces changes
  - some changes benign; original passing tests identify meaningful faults; failure diagnosis gives bug type
  - challenge objective: both components useful for industry; tracker = diverse real-world; injection = project-specific bugs hard to learn from general data
- Sources and results
  - NVD: vulnerability data in SCAP; security checklist references, software flaws, misconfigurations, product names, impact metrics
  - OSS-Fuzz by Google: open source continuous fuzzing, random inputs, security vulnerabilities/defects in OSS
  - injector: 16 single-statement rules from previous work (cite)
  - total 1 057 818 bugs from 2 968 projects = PreciseBugs; 12 602 from tracker, 1 045 216 from injector
  - largest executable bug dataset with precise bug info to our knowledge
  - contributions: tool; PreciseBugs across more than six languages; open at https://github.com/SophieHYe/PreciseBugs

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Having a precise bug dataset is crucial for many software tasks, like bug detection, fault localization, pattern mining, automated program repair for generating patches, and patch assessment. The current bug datasets can be put into two main types. The first type is curated by humans, which gives carefully processed but small datasets, for example ManyBugs and IntroClass, Defects4J and QuixBugs. All of them have fewer than 1 000 bugs each. The second type is large-scale datasets mined from code repositories, for example ManySStubBs4J, which process commit messages or issues with text processing. But this way of doing it is usually imprecise for identifying bugs or classifying their types, because it relies on simple keyword comparison. Even with this loss of precision, crawling historical bug-fix commits from open-source projects is still a very common way to collect bug-fix training data, both in academia and in industry, because it makes it easy to build large-scale datasets.

Collecting a bug dataset that is really useful and precise has several key challenges:

- Problem 1 - Data quality and scalability: Collecting manually gives a good quality dataset but it does not scale. Collecting automatically with keyword matching on commits scales, but it is imprecise.

- Problem 2 - Language diversity: Most datasets only have one language, which limits how usable they are and is a threat to the external validity of software tasks.

- Problem 3 - Lack of metadata: Usually the only metadata a dataset gives for a bug is a commit ID or commit message. Important information like the type of bug, how severe it is and when it was discovered is missing.

- Problem 4 - Lack of tests: Only a few bug datasets have test cases for the exposed bug. This makes it hard to reproduce the bug, and also to validate bug fixes other than the one from the developer.

In this paper we introduce PreciseBugCollector, a new approach to tackle the imprecision problem when creating bug datasets. Our approach gives a curated collection of software defects, with accurate bug type classification and also meta information describing the bug, including the original buggy code, the fix code, the precise location, the error type, and executable/reproducible test cases when they are available. We write this information as <bug,fix,loc,type,(test)>.

PreciseBugCollector has two components: a bug tracker for collecting general bugs, and bug injection for generating project-specific bugs. The bug tracker extracts bug-fix commits, using available code repositories (e.g., GitHub, Bitbucket, Gitlab, SVN) and external bug repositories (e.g., OSS-Fuzz, Jira, Apache Bug Report). Code repositories give the exact source code changes that were made to fix bugs, and bug repositories give detailed metadata about each bug. But looking at each repository on its own is incomplete. Code repositories have the source code changes but no clear bug metadata, and bug repositories do not always have the exact source code changes. So we devise a method that merges the two sources and gets the advantages of both.

- Bug injection
  - generates artificial unseen bugs, each exposed by existing test suite with at least one failing test
  - start from code with all tests passing; code noising tool introduces changes
  - some changes benign; original passing tests identify meaningful faults; failure diagnosis gives bug type
  - challenge objective: both components useful for industry; tracker = diverse real-world; injection = project-specific bugs hard to learn from general data
- Sources and results
  - NVD: vulnerability data in SCAP; security checklist references, software flaws, misconfigurations, product names, impact metrics
  - OSS-Fuzz by Google: open source continuous fuzzing, random inputs, security vulnerabilities/defects in OSS
  - injector: 16 single-statement rules from previous work
  - total 1 057 818 bugs from 2 968 projects = PreciseBugs; 12 602 from tracker, 1 045 216 from injector
  - largest executable bug dataset with precise bug info to our knowledge
  - contributions: tool; PreciseBugs across more than six languages; open at https://github.com/SophieHYe/PreciseBugs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Having a precise bug dataset is crucial for many software tasks, like bug detection, fault localization, pattern mining, automated program repair for generating patches, and patch assessment. The current bug datasets can be put into two main types. The first type is curated by humans, which gives carefully processed but small datasets, for example ManyBugs and IntroClass, Defects4J and QuixBugs. All of them have fewer than 1 000 bugs each. The second type is large-scale datasets mined from code repositories, for example ManySStubBs4J, which process commit messages or issues with text processing. But this way of doing it is usually imprecise for identifying bugs or classifying their types, because it relies on simple keyword comparison. Even with this loss of precision, crawling historical bug-fix commits from open-source projects is still a very common way to collect bug-fix training data, both in academia and in industry, because it makes it easy to build large-scale datasets.

Collecting a bug dataset that is really useful and precise has several key challenges:

- Problem 1 - Data quality and scalability: Collecting manually gives a good quality dataset but it does not scale. Collecting automatically with keyword matching on commits scales, but it is imprecise.

- Problem 2 - Language diversity: Most datasets only have one language, which limits how usable they are and is a threat to the external validity of software tasks.

- Problem 3 - Lack of metadata: Usually the only metadata a dataset gives for a bug is a commit ID or commit message. Important information like the type of bug, how severe it is and when it was discovered is missing.

- Problem 4 - Lack of tests: Only a few bug datasets have test cases for the exposed bug. This makes it hard to reproduce the bug, and also to validate bug fixes other than the one from the developer.

In this paper we introduce PreciseBugCollector, a new approach to tackle the imprecision problem when creating bug datasets. Our approach gives a curated collection of software defects, with accurate bug type classification and also meta information describing the bug, including the original buggy code, the fix code, the precise location, the error type, and executable/reproducible test cases when they are available. We write this information as <bug,fix,loc,type,(test)>.

PreciseBugCollector has two components: a bug tracker for collecting general bugs, and bug injection for generating project-specific bugs. The bug tracker extracts bug-fix commits, using available code repositories (e.g., GitHub, Bitbucket, Gitlab, SVN) and external bug repositories (e.g., OSS-Fuzz, Jira, Apache Bug Report). Code repositories give the exact source code changes that were made to fix bugs, and bug repositories give detailed metadata about each bug. But looking at each repository on its own is incomplete. Code repositories have the source code changes but no clear bug metadata, and bug repositories do not always have the exact source code changes. So we devise a method that merges the two sources and gets the advantages of both.

Bug injection generates artificial unseen bugs automatically, and each bug is specified by an existing test suite where at least one failing test exposes it. To start generating bugs, we take code extracted from various projects and make sure all the existing tests pass. Then the code noising tool is used to deliberately introduce changes into this code, which simulates bug injection. Not all of the injected code is really buggy, since some changes can be benign, so we use the original passing tests to identify the injected faults that are meaningful. The test failure diagnosis we get from this validation identifies precisely the type of bug that was introduced.

Given the challenge objective, we think bugs from both the bug tracker and the bug injection components are useful in industrial settings. The bug tracker gives us access to a diverse range of bug fixes from real-world projects, which makes the dataset more representative. Bug injection gives us project-specific bugs, which are hard to learn from a general dataset, tailored for industrial settings.

For the bug tracker we use two bug tracking sources: the National Vulnerability Dataset (NVD) and OSS-Fuzz. NVD is a repository of vulnerability management data represented with the Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP), and it includes databases of security checklist references, software flaws, misconfigurations, product names and impact metrics. OSS-Fuzz is an open source continuous fuzzing service provided by Google. It uses random inputs (fuzzed data) to find potential vulnerabilities, bugs or crashes, and it is designed specifically to identify security vulnerabilities and defects in open-source projects. The bug injector is implemented with 16 single-statement injection rules from previous work.

So far, PreciseBugCollector has collected 1 057 818 bugs in total from 2 968 open-source projects. We call this dataset PreciseBugs. 12 602 of these bugs come from the bug tracker (NVD and OSS-Fuzz), and 1 045 216 bugs are generated by the bug injector. As far as we know, this is the largest executable bug dataset with precise bug information compared to related work.

Our contributions are:

- We introduce PreciseBugCollector to collect a precise bug dataset, with general real-world bug-fix data and project-specific bug-fix data.

- We present PreciseBugs, a comprehensive dataset of 1 057 818 bugs from 2 968 open-source projects in more than six programming languages.

- We make the dataset openly available to the community at https://github.com/SophieHYe/PreciseBugs.

A precise bug dataset plays a crucial role in various software tasks, including bug detection [1,2], fault localization [3,4,5,6], pattern mining [7,8,9,10], automated program repair for patch generation [11,12,13,14,15,16], and patch assessment [17,18,19,20]. Current bug datasets fall into two main types. The first type relies on human curation, resulting in carefully processed but small-scale datasets, such as ManyBugs and IntroClass [21], Defects4J [22] and QuixBugs [23], each of which contains fewer than 1 000 bugs. The second type comprises large-scale datasets mined from code repositories, such as ManySStubBs4J [24], which processes commit messages or issues with text processing. However, this approach tends to be imprecise in identifying bugs or classifying their types, as it relies on simple keyword comparison. Despite this loss of precision, crawling historical bug-fix commits from open-source projects remains a widely used approach to collecting bug-fix training data in both academia [25,26] and industry [27,28], due to the ease with which it can construct large-scale datasets.

There are several key challenges to collecting a truly useful, precise bug dataset:

- Problem 1 - Data quality and scalability: Manual collection ensures the quality of the dataset but does not scale. Automatic collection with keyword matching on commits scales, but is imprecise [29].

- Problem 2 - Language diversity: Most datasets cover only a single language, limiting their usability and threatening the external validity of software tasks.

- Problem 3 - Lack of metadata: The most common metadata provided per bug is a commit ID or commit message. Important information such as the type of bug, its severity, and the date of discovery is missing.

- Problem 4 - Lack of tests: Only a handful of bug datasets provide test cases for the exposed bug. This hampers both bug reproduction and the validation of bug fixes beyond the one provided by the developer.

In this paper, we introduce PreciseBugCollector, a novel approach to tackling the imprecision problem in bug dataset creation. Our approach offers a curated collection of software defects, providing not only accurate bug type classification but also meta information describing each bug, including the original buggy code, fix code, precise location, error type, and available executable/reproducible test cases. We denote this information as <bug,fix,loc,type,(test)>.

PreciseBugCollector is based on two components: a bug tracker for general bug collection, and bug injection for project-specific bug generation. The bug tracker extracts bug-fix commits, leveraging available code repositories (e.g., GitHub, Bitbucket, Gitlab, SVN) and external bug repositories (e.g., OSS-Fuzz, Jira, Apache Bug Report). The code repositories provide the exact source code changes made to address bugs, while the bug repositories offer detailed metadata about each bug. However, considering each repository in isolation is incomplete: code repositories contain source code changes but lack clear bug metadata, and bug repositories do not always include the exact source code changes. We therefore devise a method to merge these two sources, combining the advantages of both.

Bug injection automatically generates artificial unseen bugs, each specified by an existing test suite with at least one failing test that exposes the bug. To start the bug generation process, we take code extracted from various projects and ensure that all existing tests pass. The code noising tool is then used to deliberately introduce changes into this code, simulating bug injection. Not all injected code is genuinely buggy, as some changes may be benign, so we use the original passing tests to identify meaningful injected faults. The test failure diagnosis obtained through this validation precisely identifies the type of bug introduced.

Considering the challenge objective, we regard bugs from both the bug tracker and the bug injection components as beneficial for industrial settings. The bug tracker gives us access to a diverse range of bug fixes from real-world projects, making the dataset more representative. Bug injection provides project-specific bugs that are difficult to learn from a general dataset and are tailored to industrial settings.

The bug tracker uses two bug tracking sources: the National Vulnerability Dataset (NVD) and OSS-Fuzz. NVD is a repository of vulnerability management data represented using the Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP); it includes databases of security checklist references, software flaws, misconfigurations, product names, and impact metrics. OSS-Fuzz, provided by Google, is an open source continuous fuzzing service that uses random inputs (fuzzed data) to discover potential vulnerabilities, bugs, or crashes; it is specifically designed to identify security vulnerabilities and defects in open-source projects. We implement the bug injector with 16 single-statement injection rules from previous work [30].

To date, PreciseBugCollector has collected a total of 1 057 818 bugs from 2 968 open-source projects, a dataset we name PreciseBugs. Of these, 12 602 bugs come from the bug tracker (NVD and OSS-Fuzz), while 1 045 216 bugs are generated by the bug injector. To our knowledge, this is the largest executable bug dataset with precise bug information compared with related work.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

- We introduce PreciseBugCollector for collecting a precise bug dataset of both general real-world bug-fix data and project-specific bug-fix data.

- We present a comprehensive dataset named PreciseBugs, which includes 1 057 818 bugs from 2 968 open-source projects across more than six programming languages.

- We make our dataset openly available to the community at https://github.com/SophieHYe/PreciseBugs.
